content: Emergency intubation is widely recognized as a critical, life-saving procedure for patients experiencing severe acute illness or injury, particularly when their airway or ventilation is compromised or at risk. However, some initial studies have questioned whether this intervention consistently provides significant benefits. The objective of this review was to assess whether emergency endotracheal intubation, compared to other airway management techniques, improves outcomes in acutely ill or injured patients. Specifically, the review aimed to evaluate survival rates, levels of disability at discharge, hospital length of stay, and in-hospital complications. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, covering studies up to December 2006. Non-English publications were also included, and experts in the field were consulted. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or controlled clinical trials involving emergency endotracheal intubation in acutely ill or injured patients. A total of 452 studies were initially identified, and their full texts were independently reviewed by two authors. Disagreements regarding study inclusion were resolved collectively. Due to significant variability in patient populations, practitioners, and alternative airway management techniques, the results were not combined into a meta-analysis. Three eligible RCTs were identified, all conducted in urban settings. Two trials involved adults with non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. In one trial, patients who underwent physician-operated intubation showed a non-significant survival disadvantage compared to those managed with a combi-tube (relative risk [RR] 0.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.09 to 1.99). The second trial found a non-significant survival disadvantage for paramedic intubation compared to the use of an esophageal gastric airway (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.90). The third study focused on children requiring airway intervention in prehospital settings. It found no significant differences in survival (odds ratio [OR] 0.82, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.11) or neurological outcomes (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.22) between paramedic intubation and bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation followed by hospital intubation by emergency physicians. Notably, only 42% of children randomized to paramedic intubation actually received the intervention. The authors concluded that the effectiveness of emergency intubation, as it is currently practiced, has not been rigorously evaluated. The skill level of the operator appears to play a critical role in determining the success of the procedure. In cases of non-traumatic cardiac arrest, emergency intubation is unlikely to provide the same life-saving benefits as early defibrillation and bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). For trauma and pediatric patients, the current evidence does not support expanding the use of prehospital intubation in urban systems. The authors recommend conducting a large, high-quality randomized trial to compare the efficacy of competently performed emergency intubation with basic bag-valve-mask ventilation in urban adult patients experiencing out-of-hospital non-traumatic cardiac arrest.
